articles.title: British GT Silverstone 500 live on Sky Sports F1: Sky Tempesta Racing aim for glory in new Ferrari
articles.summary: Watch the Silverstone 500 live this weekend on Sky Sports F1 ; Qualifying on Saturday from 3.50pm with race coverage on Sunday starting at midday; Sky Tempesta Racing debuting their new Ferrari 296 GT3 car on home ground in field of more than 40 entries for the three-hour sportscar race
articles.body:
The team are returning to British GT's showpiece event at the home of British motorsport and will race their all-new Ferrari 296 GT3.

This year, Sky Tempesta Racing have swapped McLaren for Ferrari machinery with their entry being overseen by the latter's prestigious AF Corse factory sportscar squad.

It will be the first time since 2020 that Ferrari have featured in the top class of the Silverstone 500 field.

Sky Tempesta and driver Chris Froggatt missed out on victory in last season's Silver-Am British GT standings by a single point, and are hopeful of a competitive weekend as they chase class honours at Silverstone.

"I'm very happy to be back in the British GT paddock, and especially at my favourite British circuit," said Froggatt, who is joined by new team-mate Alexander West.

"And I am also looking forward to sharing the 296 GT3 with Alex, who was on the opposite side of our British GT garage last year.

"I feel like we have a good foundation from which we can challenge the other Silver-Am crews."

Sky Tempesta arrive at Silverstone after finishing fourth in class in the opening round of the GT World Challenge Europe at France's Paul Ricard at the start of April.

"It is great being back in British GT for my favourite race of the season at Silverstone," said West. "Having previously raced the fantastic 488 GT3 I am really looking forward to trying the latest Ferrari with Sky Tempesta."

There are more than 40 entries across the GT3 and GT4 classes for the showpiece weekend, the third round of the 2024 British GT campaign, with supercars from manufacturers including Mercedes, Aston Martin, and McLaren.

Sky Sports F1 is airing live coverage of both Saturday's qualifying session and Sunday's three-hour race.

articles.title: Leyton Orient boss Richie Wellens and The Punjabi O's discuss the signings of Dilan Markanday and Sonny Perkins and why representation matters
articles.summary: Leyton Orient manager Richie Wellens meets the founder of The Punjabi O's Arvi Sahota and explains why he signed South Asian trailblazers Dilan Markanday and Sonny Perkins; watch Leyton Orient vs Stevenage live on Sky Sports Football from 7.30pm on Thursday
articles.body:
English football has failed to make meaningful progress in addressing the long-term under-representation of British South Asians in the game, with significantly less than one per cent of professionally contracted footballers hailing from the community - who remain the UK's single-largest ethnic minority group.

Orient boss Wellens - who shared a dressing-room with former Newcastle United and Cardiff City striker Michael Chopra during a brief loan spell with Ipswich in his playing days - has proved as a head coach that he is prepared to give top South Asian talent a chance.

Wellens managed Pakistan international and former Manchester United youngster Otis Khan in his first season as Orient boss - and has signed fellow British South Asians Sonny Perkins and Dilan Markanday this term, with the latter joining on loan from Blackburn after a successful first half of the campaign at Chesterfield.

Ahead of Thursday night's League One visit of Stevenage, live on Sky Sports, Wellens welcomed Arvi Sahota - the founder of official Leyton Orient supporters' group The Punjabi O's - to the club's training ground.

"Sonny's got a lot of talent," Wellens explains. "He was a wonderkid at West Ham.

"Then he got a move to Leeds. I think he's had something like 14 goal contributions this year in his first season. That's not bad, Sonny is a good football player.

"And then we obviously had a problem with injuries to Dan Agyei and Ollie O'Neill, and Dilan Markanday was having a brilliant season.

"I've watched Dilan loads for Tottenham and for Blackburn, and he was having a really good season at Chesterfield [that's why I signed him].

The Leyton Orient manager continued: "Also, the amount of South Asian players that must live within a five-hour radius (of the club).

"If they see a Dilan Markanday, who plays for Leyton Orient, or a Sonny Perkins, they'll want to play. Mal Benning [at Shrewsbury Town for example] has also been around for a long time.

"But they have to be good enough. Then it's just like a snowball effect.

"And when they see people they can aspire to, you know what they do? They practice more because they want to be like them and that's what makes the standard go up."

articles.title: Brian Carney's Ashes reflections: Shaun Wane and the burden of his own benchmark for England
articles.summary: Following England's 3-0 Ashes loss to Australia, Sky Sports Rugby League's Brian Carney shares his reflections...
articles.body:
Wane in February 2020 said: "If I don't get to a World Cup final and win, it's a disaster. We haven't beaten Australia for a long time and I'm embarrassed by that. And if we don't beat them, it's on me."

In the end, Wane didn't just set the bar, he fashioned the trapdoor beneath it. Those were his words, not anyone else's.

And by his own measure, the two most important campaigns of his six years in charge have been nothing short of catastrophic.

England's home World Cup, played in 2022 not 2021 because of Covid, was supposed to be the moment rugby league reconnected with a wider domestic audience. The draw was deliberately kind: no Australia, no New Zealand until the final. All roads led to Old Trafford.

Except, of course, England didn't make it there.

They were beaten in the semis by Samoa- a Samoan side England had blitzed in the tournament's opening game.

Many good judges feel it was a semi-final that was there for the taking. England went in as favourites and came unstuck in a big way.

By Wane's 2020 logic, not winning the final would have been a "disaster". What words would one use to describe not even making it?

Fast forward to 2025 and Australia return for the first Ashes series in years.

A golden chance again for the game on these shores to fire up the sporting public's imagination. Instead, the Kangaroos left with a clean sweep and England barely left clutching the usual consolation prize of "effort".

Three defeats, three below-par performances, just two tries in 240 minutes of rugby league. If Wane was embarrassed in 2020 about England not beating Australia in so long, he must be incandescent now.

I watched Reece Walsh sign autographs pitchside an hour after the final whistle on Saturday. The Australians, the team I'm told the English love to hate, had won the hearts and minds of supporters over here.

England's rugby league team is more than a collection of individuals sent out to win a game. They represent the sport.

For whatever reason they admirably welcomed cameras into camp for a behind-the-scenes documentary yet appeared to be kept from the cameras, microphones and adoring fans at other times. This is just my perception. No doubt a series review will determine if this was indeed the case.

The question now falls to the RFL: back him or sack him. Wane is contracted until the end of 2026, taking in next year's World Cup in Australia and Papua New Guinea. He hasn't coached a club side since 2018, an eternity in rugby league terms.

In November 2024 Wane expressed a desire to return to club coaching at some point in the future, admitting he missed preparing regularly for matches and hinting at excess capacity: "I feel like I'm under-selling myself".

The likes of Paul Rowley, Matt Peet, Willie Peters, Michael Maguire and Brian McDermott are all names likely to come to the fore in conversations about Wane's future.

Wane's prickly dismissal of the Man of Steel award did little to help his cause. Asked about Jake Connor, the 2025 winner, Wane waved it away: "I don't know who picks it and it never comes into my consideration."

You don't have to pick Jake Connor to respect the game's most prestigious individual award. But publicly diminishing it? That's poor politics.

How do the RFL market an honour their own England coach treats with contempt? There are more than enough knowledgeable rugby league fans here. I've met and spoken to them at Wembley, Headingley and in recent days at events in Hull, Keighley and Cumbria.

I'm echoing their sentiments. They demand more than a "credit in the bank" explanation when selecting players to represent them.

At times, Wane's passion seems to have curdled into obstinacy. He talks about "English grit" as if it were a secret weapon, but grit without craft is just friction.

His side looked rigid, predictable, and joyless. For a man who once demanded England "play without fear", his team look paralysed by it.

When asked recently about 2026, Wane said: "I don't believe I'm the right man to coach England at the World Cup - I know it."

He "knew" plenty of things, of course. He "knew" the out-of-form players he picked would deliver. They didn't. He "knew" his spine was right - until he changed three of those four positions after one game.

Do they double down on loyalty, or acknowledge that the "disaster" Wane once warned of has already arrived and, by his own admission, it's on him?

Because in sport, as in politics, when your own words become your best critic, the argument is usually over.

There are of course much broader issues at play in the game over here. Including their focus on the international game the RFL must decide if more of the same will deliver different results and if they are happy with keeping their fingers crossed for that.

The alternative is to draw a line in the sand and make this period the cliff edge we refused to get pushed over. The next few months will be telling.

articles.title: AFCON 2025: Rochdale winger Tarryn Allarakhia earns place in Tanzania Africa Cup of Nations squad for second time
articles.summary: Tarryn Allarakhia recounts facing Mohamed Salah on his Tanzania debut, being "humbled" by Achraf Hakimi in his first Africa Cup Of Nations game and leaving Rochdale's promotion push to play at the tournament for a second time
articles.body:
Less than two weeks later he was making his debut for Tanzania in a friendly against Egypt, facing off against Mohamed Salah, Mohamed Elneny, Trezeguet and Omar Marmoush, no less.

Allarakhia was east London born and raised; his mum is English, with his Tanzanian heritage from his dad. He was on Leyton Orient's books as a youngster, but barring three seasons at Crawley between 2018 and 2021, has otherwise played in non-League.

The 28-year-old had visited his nan and other family members in "beautiful" Tanzania a handful of times, but the level he was playing at meant playing international football was far from his mind.

That changed when he received a call from the head coach at the time, Adel Amrouche, following a conversation with Haji Mnoga, another UK-born Tanzania international, who was then on loan at Aldershot from Portsmouth.

"My name came up and the manager said he liked the way I play," Allarakhia says.

"He actually came all the way over to watch me play. That's when I knew he was really, really keen on me.

"Nothing was certain or concrete at the start, but there suggestions that it could happen. When the opportunity to play for Tanzania came up, I knew I'd love to play for them and it was something I wanted to check off the list."

Early in the new year, he flew to Cairo and on January 7 2024, replaced Simon Msuva at half-time to earn that historic first cap.

"When I stepped into the stadium, then heard the national anthem, it dawned on me I was playing international football.

"I wouldn't say it a moment where I was starstruck when I came up against all these stars, but it was like: 'Wow, I'm actually here!'

"I came on and I just thought: 'What is there to lose?' No one really knew who I was, so I just had to go out there and show what I could do.

"I had a good game as well, to be fair, so it was a successful debut.

"I did try to get Salah's shirt afterwards, but there were too many security guards so I thought I'd just leave it and take the memories!"

The whirlwind quickly continued because Allarakhia was then named in Amrouche's squad for the delayed AFCON 2023 in the Ivory Coast, alongside the aforementioned Mnoga and Ben Starkie, who spoke to Sky Sports about their own experiences in the lead-up to the tournament.

"When you're new, it's hard and, to be fair, all the boys made time for me, which helped us gel," he adds.

"But it was good to have all the European boys there. It makes a big difference and it makes you more comfortable when you've got familiar faces around you.

"If I went there on my own, I think it would have been much harder."

Just 10 days after his debut, Allarakhia started on the left wing in what was only the Taifa Stars' seventh AFCON match, against Morocco.

"In Egypt I didn't get starstruck, but at AFCON, that's where I was like: 'Wow. This is mad. I'm here.'

"But that game didn't go as good as the first one. I got humbled by Achraf Hakimi, the best right-back in the world.

"It was a great learning curve. The climate didn't help, going from playing in England to playing in 40-degree heat, but I made sure I took every single bit I could learn from that game to help me be ready for the next one."

Allarakhia was on the bench for the next two group games, by which point Hemed Morocco had been installed as caretaker, with Amrouche suspended by the Tanzania Football Federation (TFF).

The Algerian coach had been handed an eight-match ban and a $10,000 fine by the Confederation of African Football (CAF). A TFF statement said he had made comments about "Morocco having influence in CAF, to manipulate the match scheduling and officiating".

Tanzania exited AFCON 2023 at the group stages, but did so respectably, given the disruption behind the scenes, having lost 3-0 to Morocco, drawn 1-1 with Zambia and 0-0 with DR Congo.

Allarakhia earned his third cap when he played in a 1-0 friendly defeat to Bulgaria in March 2024, but was not part of the national team set-up again for more than 18 months.

That was until October, when coach Morocco recalled him for a World Cup qualifier against Zambia and a friendly against Iran.

"At AFCON, I didn't really hit the ground running like against Egypt, so maybe he just thought having a little break from it would help a little bit - and to be fair, I think it actually did," Allarakhia says.

"I had a really good camp. A very positive camp. That's why I feel like now it's time to kick on."

In November, he returned to Cairo for a friendly against Kuwait where he scored his first international goal in style. He collected a square ball in the D, took a neat touch and fired into the top right corner.

On December 9, Allarakhia was named in the squad for AFCON 2025 by Miguel Gamondi - the new permanent Tanzania head coach.

He is determined to seized this second opportunity.

"Even though that first AFCON didn't go as I wanted to, football changes very quickly. There's another opportunity now where I can redeem myself. I'm older, a bit wiser and I feel stronger and fitter.

"Honestly, it would mean the world to me if I can help my country go far in a major tournament, especially when we're the underdogs. It just makes it better.

"We've got a tough group, but hopefully I could be the difference going forward."

The trade-off is temporarily leaving Rochdale's promotion push. Dale are top of the National League at the time of writing, with three games in hand, and Allarakhia has chipped in with three goals and one assist so far.

"We're in a promotion push and I am still part of that. Playing for your country is a big thing and Rochdale have been very good to me. They're encouraging me to go."

He will be hoping that the confidence gained from domestic football will play an important role in impressing in front of the eyes of the world.

articles.title: Jess Thirlby's departure as England Netball head coach is strange timing ahead of Commonwealth Games, says Tamsin Greenway
articles.summary: Former England international Tamsin Greenway reacts to Jess Thirlby stepping down as head coach ahead of the Commonwealth Games and discusses England's long-term options: "I think they would be naïve to think this is the only group that can take that team forward."
articles.body:
It was announced on Tuesday that Thirlby is stepping down from her role with immediate effect after nearly seven years in charge. Her departure comes just four months out from the Commonwealth Games.

Thirlby referenced a desire to focus on supporting her family as a primary reason for her decision, as Anna Stembridge steps up from assistant coach to oversee England's upcoming campaign in Glasgow.

Last month England fell to a 2-1 series defeat against South Africa, in what turned out to be Thirlby's final act as head coach.

"There have been rumblings coming off the back of playing South Africa bearing in mind we have to play them in the pool round of the Commonwealth Games, and Australia, which are two massive games," former England international Greenway told Sky Sports.

"As an England fan looking at it in the background, it's been a rollercoaster ride. There have been some incredible moments in her six-and-a-half years, the Netball World Cup final, that was ground-breaking.

"You only have to go back 12 months previous and we didn't medal at the last Commonwealth Games, so it's been very up and down.

"It does seem to strange to do it now, there have been bigger and different opportunities where it probably could have happened to give the new coaching team a longer lead up to a big competition.

"But coming off the back of that South Africa series they probably didn't feel like it could continue."

England failed to medal at the Commonwealth Games in 2022 having entered as defending champions in the wake of their 2018 glory.

Greenway recalled being part of the 2015 squad that competed at the World Cup in the wake of a coaching change, Stembridge also stepping into the role on that occasion. So while there comes the prospect of disruption, there also is the possibility of fresh impetus.

"It was what we needed, it freshened it up, it was probably what the group needed, the group was good enough but it just needed a different outlook," she said.

"I think it's similar now. This is a group of athletes that could very well go and win the gold medal.

"If it is just a cultural piece, about miscommunication between players and staff, they've lost a bit of trust, then actually it could be the freshen-up they need.

"But it is a risk. You've kept a group of coaches in there that have been in this regime so they have to get to the bottom of this, understand what the players need and work out very quickly what this campaign will look like."

Stembridge previously served as England head coach from 2011 to 2015 and led the side to gold at the World Netball Series in Liverpool in her first year. Her staff introduces former Roses captain Olivia Murphy as an assistant coach on a secondment from Loughborough Sport, with Sharni Layton and Jo Harten as specialist coaches.

"She was there, she has been in the mix, she's done it before," said Greenway of Stembridge. "You can't really go overseas with a new group. It is a risk when you do this. I think it's getting to the bottom of why it's happened.

"We've had incredible games overseas against Australia and New Zealand and then lost the South Africa series 2-1. If you want to compete at the world stage that consistency matters.

"If you are going to move the coach at this point or if she is going to step away you have to have some level of consistency going into this competition.

"They'll be some big names in there. Liv Murphy, who has played at the top level and masterminded Loughborough Lightning's success for many years. Of course Sharni Layton and Jo Harten, two key internationals who the players will respect a lot."

While Stembridge represents a proven option, Greenway believes Thirlby's decision to step aside offers England an opportunity to consider a fresh direction for a win-ready group of players in the long term.

"They've got a year to build-up to the World Cup and they need to decide what they actually want here and what is the building ground," said Greenway.

"To her credit Jess Thirlby has brought through the likes of Liv Tchine, Funmi Fadoju, the leadership of Fran Williams. These have become world class players on the world stage, but I think now is the opportunity to rip the band-aid off on the back of the Commonwealth Games and go 'what is it we're looking for now?'.

"Now we've got a professional Super League, how can we integrate that programme better? And who are the coaches out there?

"In Anna Stembridge's defence, she has been there and done it, but she hasn't actually been a head coach for a very long time and it will be interesting because when it gets round to the Commonwealth Games they will be in goal-for-goal matches and high-pressure situations, that bench will have to make some cutthroat decisions.

"I think they have to wait for the Commonwealth Games, but I think they would be naïve to think this is the only group that can take that team forward."

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: Gracie Smith and Sophie Kelly likely to be omitted from England netball squad, says Tracey Neville
articles.summary: Gracie Smith and Sophie Kelly are set to miss out on the Commonwealth Games due to logistical issues and competition; Watch the Netball Super League live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Speaking on the Off the Court podcast, Neville bemoaned the challenges that come from including inexperienced players like Smith and Kelly in the squad, citing competition for places and logistics as key obstacles to their inclusion.

"About three to four months out, you have to put your long listing of 18 to 22 players. That's actually quite scary because one, that risks injuries," Neville said.

"And at Commonwealth Games, you can't replace injuries like you can at a World Cup.

"And then secondly, you also don't have time for people like Sophie Kelly or Gracie Smith, if they've not been part of that full-time program.

"I look at someone like Smith, who's been absolutely outstanding by the way. To have a centre of her calibre come through is just been exceptional. But even from my point of view now, I look at it and I go, that squad list went in a little bit ago.

"She's actually got no chance of ever getting in that Commonwealth Games, irrespective of performance."

Even without the logistical challenges facing the squad selection before the Games, Neville believes that midcourt competition is simply too strong to allow a budding star like Smith any gametime.

"I also look at who would I drop for Gracie Smith.

"I actually collectively put down about 18 to 20 names and my midcourt at the moment, based on what's gone before us, what we've learned is people like Amy Carter - would I drop her? No. Imogen Allison? No. Beth Givhan, Jess Shaw, Nat Metcalf, Alicia Scholes...

"I probably would not have dropped any of them for Gracie Smith, irrespective of her having the most unbelievable season.

"In a way, people need to respect that these decisions have to be made quite early, but they also have to be made off the back of what has gone before as well.

"And that's something that is really hard to get your head around and one as a fan, because potentially these rules are not put out to the public. It's the long-term planning, isn't it? Grace is just another example.

"There are so many U21s coming through that are having great seasons or will be the future of netball."

articles.title: England netball star Helen Housby ruled out of this summer's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with back injury
articles.summary: England will be without Helen Housby for the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow; experienced goal shooter suffered a back injury in April; watch the Netball Super League live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The Games are set to take place in Glasgow from July 23 until August 2, but England will be without their mainstay goal shooter.

In April it was revealed that Housby would miss an "extended period" of the Suncorp Super Netball season in Australia due to a back injury, with further scans confirming she will be unable to compete this summer.

Housby, who famously scored England's last-minute winner when they won gold at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, says she is "devastated" to miss out in the Glasgow event.

"Representing Team England is an honour and holds some of my proudest and fondest memories," she said.

"Despite the setback I'm more determined than ever to come back stronger and get back on court as soon as possible, especially with the World Cup in Sydney on the horizon.

"I'm lucky to be surrounded by an incredible support system and I'm very grateful for the love I've received from those closest to me, England Netball, the New South Wales Swifts and the Vitality Roses fans back home.

"I'm excited to see what our girls can achieve this summer and will be giving everything I can off the court to support them in Glasgow. I truly believe our squad can beat anybody and I'm looking forward to watching as a fan this time around."

articles.title: Netball Super League: Chelsea Pitman on Nottingham Forest Netball, the Super League semi-finals and 'Pavlova'
articles.summary: Nottingham Forest Netball have sealed a play-off place with two games to go in the Netball Super League; head coach Chelsea Pitman has eyes on glory; watch the Netball Super League live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Forest will play Loughborough Lightning in the minor semi-final on Saturday June 6 - who they beat in round 12 to secure their place in the play-offs - while Manchester Thunder and reigning champions London Pulse will go head-to-head in the major semi-final.

The winner of the major semi-final secures an automatic place in the Grand Final at Co-op Live in Manchester on June 20. The loser will then take on the winner of the minor semi-final to determine who claims the second spot in the final.

"I think back to when we got together in October - planning for this season - and saying that it would be amazing to reach top four in just our second season," said Forest head coach and former World Cup winner Chelsea Pitman, who has been at the helm since their inception in 2024.

"To achieve that with two games to go is such a remarkable feat.

"They know how to win, but we are still building - being able to control the game was great to see."

Two players who have been at the heart of everything good about Forest this season are Jayda Pechova and Natasha Pavelin.

They have been expertly nicknamed 'Pavlova' by the Forest fans - and the mere mention of the dynamic duo instantly brought a smile to Pitman's face.

"The pairing between Tash and Jayda has grown and grown, they live together so everything is coming along nicely at the right time.

"They absolutely batter our attackers in training, they train how they play and it's a testament to what we are building here.

"I love their nickname and with Commonwealth Games selection looming it's a big plus for England Netball and those two are putting their hands up for selection."

Formed in 2024 as part of the Nottingham Forest franchise, the club has benefited enormously from the professional infrastructure and elite training environment that come with links to a Premier League side - so much so that Pitman now describes herself as an adopted Forest fan.

"Being Australian I never really had a soft spot for a football club before, but even the way they have been with a sort of muck in mentality and how they have been in every aspect on the netball side has been nothing short of incredible."

With both semi-finals potentially being away, Pitman has called on "as many reds fans" as possible to come and support the team, who are now three games away from Super League history.

articles.title: Zidane Iqbal interview: Iraq's former Man Utd midfielder on World Cup dreams, Cristiano Ronaldo and much more
articles.summary: In this exclusive interview with Sky Sports, Iraq midfielder Zidane Iqbal discusses what it means to help the country qualify for their first World Cup in 40 years, his memories of Manchester United and how he is hoping to upset the odds at this summer's tournament
articles.body:
That 1986 appearance was long before his time. "The 2010 World Cup is the first I can remember." Not even the headbutt by his namesake Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 final? "I have seen the clips but I was only three!" Now Iraq get to make memories of their own.

"The amount of messages, the support we have had is crazy." Iqbal, now playing for Utrecht but born and raised in Manchester, is eligible through his Iraqi mother and has become a firm favourite having scored a crucial goal against Indonesia during qualifying.

"Honestly, it was an unbelievable feeling," he recalls. "It was just surreal scoring that goal because that is what I was waiting for." Unfortunately, that alone was not enough to get Iraq to the World Cup. They still needed a play-off win over Bolivia to end their exile.

Iqbal sat that game out on the bench. Just back from long-term injury, the coach only planned to use him if absolutely necessary. As it is, his team-mates got the job done. He actually found it harder to watch. "When you are playing, the adrenaline takes over."

The celebrations were special with Iqbal donning a sombrero that night in Mexico amid joyous scenes. He talks of the Iraq team being "one big family" and receiving messages from around the world. He understands that this can be a life-changing experience.

As a result, the focus since has been on getting himself in peak condition for the World Cup. "Making sure I can be at 100 per cent." Even on his days off, he has been having one-on-one sessions in Manchester, determined to ensure it is a summer to remember.

Iraq will have to be workmanlike at this World Cup but Iqbal is the one capable of providing the spark. "I like to play football," he says. "I like to dribble. I like to play forward and link up the play." That is what took him all the way to the Manchester United first team.

Iqbal signed for Manchester United at the age of eight and spent a dozen years at the club. "I can say that I lived my childhood dream," he says. In 2021, at the age of just 18, he made his first-team debut in the Champions League against Young Boys.

"It was probably one of the best days of my life," he admits. "I did not expect to come on. I just thought I would warm up, sit down and watch the game." Instead, he was introduced for the final moments. "The ball took forever to go out as well!" And made history.

Iqbal was not only the first South Asian to play for United but the first to play in the Champions League. "I just focused on football, not to be the first of this or that, just because it was a dream of mine," he admits. "But it is nice knowing that you can inspire kids."

While that taste of first-team action at United was the obvious highlight, the pinnacle of his career at the club, it was the day-to-day experiences that have stayed with him too. Iqbal had the opportunity to train alongside an all-time great in Cristiano Ronaldo.

"Seeing someone that you had played with on FIFA and stuff to then train with was crazy. Just watching and trying to learn from him, just him being around. It is hard to describe because he is probably one of the greatest of all time, if not the greatest."

What has he taken from seeing Ronaldo work? "Just his mentality, how focused he is, how seriously he takes things. But he is also a very nice, calm guy. When people ask me how he is and does he speak to the guys, he does. He is like everyone else. He is chill."

The decision to leave Manchester United was his own. A loan move was an option but Iqbal was ready for the next step. "I thought I needed to go out somewhere and prove myself." The Netherlands just felt right. "The best league for me to go to. Technical."

His time at Utrecht has been disrupted by two injuries. "But I have come back stronger from both of them." Importantly, he has been exposed to the sort of experiences, both in the Eredivisie and in Europe, that have accelerated his game to the next level.

"It is a lot different," he explains. "The stadiums are full. You are playing for points. There is more pressure from the fans to perform. If you do not play well then you are going to know about it. When you are playing for the U21s, it is family and friends in the stands."

For instance, he adds: "Our tunnel to the changing room has glass windows on each side, so we can see the fans. If you are losing at half-time or not having a good game, some players can get some abuse. I have matured a lot as a player and as a person."

It is that off-field aspect that has tested him most. Moving abroad just after turning 20 was a massive step. "When you get there, reality hits you. You need to do this and that. The cereal and the milk in the fridge is not just going to be there at the weekend."

Now 23 years old, he is open about the fact that it has been challenging. "When you wake up on your day off and the house is empty, that is the main thing." But he is proud of the way that he taken on that challenge. "Living by myself, I have grown up a lot."

After three years away, the call of home is growing. Iqbal has one year left on his deal but a return to England is a possibility. "I just miss it here. We will see what happens." However, before all that, there is the small matter of the greatest show on earth.

The draw was not necessarily kind. "We have got the group of death," says Iqbal with a wry smile. Iraq begin their campaign against Erling Haaland's Norway before taking on the might of France. "Their team is amazing." The final group game is against Senegal.

Iraq coach Graham Arnold is fond of calling this schedule the group of excitement or the group of opportunity instead and that is how Iqbal likes to look at the situation too. "As a team, we are all fighters. So, we might be able to shock some people," he argues.

"No one is expecting us to get out of the group so we have got less pressure on us. I probably prefer a group like this because you get to test yourself against high-level players and you can compare your level to theirs. You always have to back yourself."

Iraq's journey to this World Cup has been an arduous one. "We have broken that 40-year curse." Now, their lad from Manchester just wants a special moment. "Football isn't played on paper. There have been upsets in the past before. Why can't we do it?"

articles.title: British South Asians in Football Team of the Season 2025/26: Hamza Choudhury, Zidane Iqbal, Yan Dhanda, Mariam Mahmood all feature
articles.summary: Sky Sports News' Dev Trehan and Desi Ballers founder Zohaib Rashid pick the fourth annual combined XI, celebrating the on-field contribution made by British South Asians in football during the 2025/2026 season
articles.body:
Players from the community featured across the leagues in men's football and at every level of the English women's football pyramid.

Nine players retain their places from last year, but how does the overrall 2025/26 team shape up?

Jasbir Singh continued to lead from the back as Tamworth vice-captain, keeping eight clean sheets across the campaign and helping the Lambs claim a top-half finish in the 2025/26 National League.

Asmita Ale makes her fourth consecutive Team of the Season appearance after a solid individual campaign. Ale played 21 Women's Super League matches across the season for Leicester City.

Danny Batth rolled back the years to play an important role for unfancied Derby County last season as the club narrowly missed out on the play-offs on the last day of the season, finishing eighth in the Sky Bet Championship.

Kam Kandola had the most productive season of his career to date, playing 38 matches in a campaign where Kidderminster Harriers clinched promotion to the National League via the play-offs. Kandola has joined Hereford ahead of the new season.

Mal Benning regained his place in Shrewsbury Town's line-up after the mid-season appointment of Gavin Cowan. Benning went on to make his 500th professional career appearance and helped the club preserve its League Two status.

Millie Chandarana became an 'Invincible' for the second consecutive season, featuring prominently as Burnley went unbeaten in the league to land the title and earn promotion to Women's Super League 2. Chandarana has just signed a new deal.

Hamza Choudhury played 32 matches for Leicester City in a difficult league campaign for the Foxes but sparkled on the international stage, scoring on his home debut for Bangladesh and instantly becoming a national hero.

Zidane Iqbal appeared in the Dutch Eredivisie and the Europa League for FC Utrecht in a season where he scored his first international goal and became the first British South Asian ever to play at a World Cup, featuring in all three of Iraq's games over the summer.

Yan Dhanda emerged as a key player for Dundee following his loan switch from Hearts, featuring in 31 matches for the club and helping the Dee comfortably retain their place in the Scottish Premiership next season.

Mariam Mahmood had a fairytale season as she made her international debut for Pakistan ahead of clinching a move to Wrexham. The club won a historic league and cup double as Mahmood became the first Pakistani female to win a top-division European title.

Dilan Markanday landed a club end-of-season Player of the Year award after scoring eight goals and contributing six assists in a season where Chesterfield narrowly missed out on a League Two play-off spot.

articles.title: Luke Littler reaches new heights with World Matchplay run to remember: 'What can other players cling onto now?'
articles.summary: Sky Sports Darts' Mark Webster believes Luke Littler produced the greatest World Matchplay campaign ever seen and has backed him to complete a clean sweep of the remaining majors in 2026
articles.body:
Littler capped off a record-breaking week with a dominant 18-9 win over Gerwyn Price in the final, setting a new record average in a final of 111.53.

He also broke his own record for the number of 180s hit across the tournament, improving his 64 in 2025 to 66 in 2026.

The victory in Blackpool saw Littler become only the fourth player in tournament history to win back-to-back titles, and the first in a decade to achieve the feat. It also keeps alive his bid to complete a clean sweep of the major titles across the year.

He already has the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League, Masters, and now the Matchplay. He is also defending the Grand Slam, Grand Prix and the Players Championship Finals later this year and hunting a European Championship win to hold every single premier title.

For Webster, Littler's run at the Matchplay marks the greatest major display in the history of the sport and is another sign that the world No 1 is increasingly likely to eventually hold every major trophy the sport has to offer simultaneously.

"This is what I keep saying - what do the other players cling on to now? Where is the weakness? What do you do," Webster said.

"He is playing fantastic at the minute and he is making his opponents miss. It is a recipe for dominance.

"The tournament average has been in the back of his mind. He is setting himself a challenge inside a challenge.

"Winning a major is a huge thing to do but he is setting little challenges within that.

"It is going to get to the point where he is going to be leaving 170s and things like that because he is dominating contests.

"He is just in a completely dominant mood. He trusts everything he does. You just have to admire it. We probably think he can't get better but he is going to try.

"He is going to keep craving tournament averages - he just has that will to win.

"This has to be the greatest campaign at a major, doesn't it? This has to be it. If you look at the stats alone, he has a tournament average of 111.

"It is an incredible achievement and it is one that in 12 months time he will try to eclipse.

"I half expect it [for him to win every major in 2026].

"I don't see where you are going to get him. European champs maybe? Players championship? I am just throwing things out there.

"It is going to be tough for the rest of them."

Time to 'take stock' as Littler sends a message to the pack

For those chasing Littler down, the question is what do you do next?

Records have fallen, he has dominated in Blackpool, and has already set his sights on what he needs to do next in order to continue this remarkable run.

And it truly is remarkable - his last defeat in a major tournament that went beyond 20 legs came against Luke Humphries in the World Darts championship back in 2024.

Can they stop what seems inevitable? Webster thinks it will take "new standards" to even get close to him.

"It just sends out a message now to the rest of the pack of the standard you have to reach to get anywhere near him.

"Every player from this event will take stock of what happened.

"Someone like Luke Humphries, it won't wash for him being knocked out in the first round so he will need to refocus.

"Michael van Gerwen has got a huge end to the year. I think he is down at world No 7 now which feels strange to say.

"There is some work for him to do there now - he was a finalist at the World Darts Championship two years ago so there is some more money coming off.

"After every tournament you have to take stock, look at what you need to improve on, and get ready for what is the business end of the year now."

The next PDC ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28-October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports . Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

The Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton (November 14-22) and the World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) are also both live on Sky Sports, with Littler looking to retain his titles in both events. Stream darts and more top sport with no contract.

articles.title: Chelsea? Liverpool? Aston Villa? Best and worst buyers and sellers of the summer transfer window - Between the Lines
articles.summary: Premier League clubs set a new spending record in a £3.4bn summer; Between the Lines applies a market adjustment to player valuations to assess the best buyers and sellers of the window and measure which clubs actually got the best value for money
articles.body:
Across the league, clubs paid around a third above Transfermarkt valuations for players in the scramble to strengthen their squads.

So, to make fairer comparisons, we've adjusted those valuations for this summer's transfer inflation, and then measured which clubs bought below that benchmark and sold above it.

It was a summer of high-profile exits for Aston Villa but they rank as the best buyers of the window according to our adjusted figures.

Our analysis shows Villa's signings had a collective value £60.0m higher than they paid. The biggest bargain was midfielder Johan Manzambi, who had an adjusted value of £74.8m at the time of his £47m move from Freiburg.

Leon Goretzka was brought in for free following the expiry of his contract at Bayern Munich but had an adjusted value of £13.8m, while Joao Gomes, Matteo Ruggeri and Zion Suzuki were also signed for fees much lower than their adjusted values.

Arsenal 's attempts to add a blockbuster attacker ended in frustration but they rank as our second-best buyers, with Piero Hincapie, signed from Bayer Leverkusen for £34.5m with an adjusted value of £57.5m, one of the best-value additions of the window.

Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimaraes and free transfer Illan Meslier also had adjusted values higher than the fees paid, giving Arsenal's signings a collective value £46.6m higher than their cost.

Chelsea's transfer policy has been criticised in recent years but the Blues come out as the third-best buyers of the window, with signings valued at £38.3m higher than their collective cost.

A large chunk of that value came from Valentin Barco, who had an adjusted value of £46.0m at the time of his £34m move from Strasbourg to Stamford Bridge, and, surprisingly, from £117m signing Morgan Rogers, who had an adjusted value of £126.6m, despite the perception that they overpaid for him.

At the other end of the scale, Newcastle rank as the worst buyers of the window in terms of finding value. Our analysis shows they overpaid for Aladji Bamba, a £35.5m signing from Monaco, to the tune of £14.8m. Matias Fernandez Pardo is also rated as a hefty overpay based on his adjusted value.

Liverpool come out as the second-worst buyers, largely because of the fees paid for Bradley Barcola and goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, which came in at £19.4m and £25.4m above value respectively.

Spurs are next on the list. Curiously, they had both the best- and worst-value signings of the summer, according to our analysis.

Marcos Senesi arrived on a free transfer from Bournemouth with an adjusted value of £28.8m, making him the joint-best-value signing alongside Leeds' Harry Wilson. But the club paid a whopping £44.7m above value with their £85m deal for Savio, an overpay which was only partially mitigated by their other signings.

Selling proved far more difficult for Premier League clubs overall, with Manchester City and Brentford the only sides in the division to emerge with positive efficiency scores for sales in our analysis.

Manchester City rank as the best sellers, having recouped £1.0m above the adjusted value of their players sold.

Their best sale was that of Savio, whose £85m move to Spurs came in £44.7m above his adjusted value, while James Trafford's £40m move to Leeds was £11.2m above value.

Brentford effectively broke even on their departures, finishing just £0.03m above the collective adjusted value of the players they sold.

Chelsea rank third, with their departure score just £0.5m below value overall.

Their best sale was that of Liam Delap, who joined Nottingham Forest for £17.8m more than his adjusted value at £50m, while the £125m sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City on Deadline Day also came in at £9.9m above value.

On the flipside, our analysis suggests Chelsea sold defenders Trevoh Chalobah and Marc Cucurella for £15.2m and £17.2m less than their respective adjusted values, ensuring that the club's departure efficiency score was not as high as it might have been.

Our data for sales is grim reading for Liverpool , who rank as the worst sellers of the summer, with their fees received coming in at £95.9m below the collective value of the departing players.

This is largely because of losing Ibrahima Konate, a player with an adjusted transfer value of £51.8m, on a free transfer, along with Andrew Robertson, who had an adjusted value of £8.1m.

But the fees received for Mohamed Salah and Curtis Jones also fell well below their values, according to our analysis.

Spurs rank as second-worst sellers, having generated £62.0m less in fees than the collective value of the players sold, with Cristian Romero, Luka Vuskovic and Djed Spence let go for £23.5m, £19.0m and £16.0m below market value respectively.

When combining signing efficiency and departure efficiency, Chelsea come out as the most efficient club of the summer in terms of finding and generating value in their purchases and sales.

Their window ended in frustration as a deal to sign Lamine Camara collapsed on Deadline Day, but their overall efficiency score of £37.7m puts them ahead of Aston Villa on £27.1m and Crystal Palace on £23.1m.

At the other end of the scale, Liverpool rank as the least efficient side of the transfer window, with an efficiency score of -£136.6m putting them below Spurs on -£81.3m and Newcastle on -£70.8m.

articles.title: Premier League transfer window: Sky Sports reporters rank your club's summer after dramatic Deadline Day
articles.summary: Sky Sports reporters rank and analyse every Premier League club's summer transfer window; top-flight clubs smashed their spending record, splashing £3.48bn on new signings
articles.body:
Eight is the number of senior players out and that's why I give Arsenal's summer business eight out of 10.

Gabriel Jesus , Gabriel Martinelli , Leandro Trossard , Christian Norgaard , Fabio Viera , Ethan Nwaneri (loan), Jakob Kiwior and Reiss Nelson are all out of the building, with the exception of Nwaneri - who still has a big future at the club - deemed surplus to requirements.

Cash in - over £100m - and wages saved. In Jesus' case, big wages.

If the club had secured a left winger to replace the two they sold, I'd have given nine out of 10. Either Vinicius Junior or Julian Alvarez coming in and it would have been a perfect 10. In the end, it wasn't to be.

Securing either was always a long shot but Arsenal deserve credit for even being in the conversation.

Fans are disappointed those two didn't come to the Emirates. But they accept it and understand.

Many, though, don't accept or understand why last season's two main left-sided attackers haven't been fully replaced. The club would have if they could have. But the right fit never emerged after the Vinicius saga.

So it's make do on the left. And the hierarchy, like Mikel Arteta , believe there's enough in the squad to do that. Newcomer Christos Tzolis , if a bit shaky last time out at Villa Park, has done well. The fans already love him.

Eberechi Eze has shown he can be impressive there as well. Also, Noni Madueke and Bukayo Saka can both do a job on the left if required.

In fact, playing one of them there is another way of giving Max Dowman more minutes. He could play down the right.

There's even a school of thought that Riccardo Calafiori could push further up the pitch. Remember Arteta finding new, unexpected roles for Mikel Merino and Myles Lewis-Skelly ?

So, no new left winger. And no new striker. But Arteta has more options everywhere else.

One look at the bench at Villa Park underlines that. Injuries allowing, Arsenal have quality depth in defence and midfield.

Total personnel changes from game to game in those areas are now possible, with little drop-off in competitiveness.

It's been a good window for Arsenal. The ones Arteta really wanted were Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa . And he got them.

When Aston Villa lifted the Europa League no one would have imagined six of the starting line-up would be departing just weeks later - least of all Unai Emery .

How do you replace Morgan Rogers , Youri Tielemans , Ollie Watkins , Emiliano Martinez , Lucas Digne, and Ezri Konsa while staying within the financial rules tightly governing the club?

The answer has been to rebuild with younger, exciting players full of potential like Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, plus some experienced heads like Leon Goretzka and Aaron Wan-Bissaka . Nicolas Jackson won't need to adapt to the league and did well on his debut on Monday night.

Zion Suzuki also made a positive first showing in goal. Taylor Harwood-Bellis says he still has plenty to improve on but is convinced the manager can help him thrive at the top level.

That Unai Emery factor has to be taken into account along with how well the club have balanced the books this summer in the face of an unwanted rebuild.

So I'm optimistic about this summer's business - with the caveat that we need real evidence of what these players can do in a Villa shirt.

Bournemouth's summer contrasted with the summer of 2025, when they sold a number of key players. This summer was about keeping their best players - and they absolutely passed the test.

Rayan , Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott all remain at the club. Bournemouth have a model that allows players to move but they also want to ensure they have those players for a chunk of time.

Bournemouth also promised Marco Rose they wouldn't sell the team from beneath him. They wanted to give him the best chance to succeed, despite strong interest in all three players.

Being in Europe changes the dynamic of what Bournemouth can spend in order to meet UEFA's financial regulations. It was a real challenge because they had to add quality and depth while reducing costs.

Bournemouth's business looks really solid. They've added a goalkeeper - Michele Di Gregorio - who was the Juventus No 1 last season. They added a centre-back - Antonio Silva - who was linked with a number of big clubs not that long ago for what looks to be great value. Juanlu Sanchez looks to be a solid full-back, and Alvaro Rodriguez looks to bring something different in attack.

Bournemouth allowed fringe players to go and one of the other positives is they were decisive, acting early in the window. They were totally comfortable which meant that - for the first time in many years - they weren't doing business on Deadline Day.

Rose and the hierarchy will look back on this as a very successful summer - now they just have to deliver on the pitch.

I'm struggling to find a reason not to give Brentford top marks on their summer business. The priority was always to bring in a dependable midfielder they could build their future around. Enter Mamadou Sangare , whose £39m price tag is looking like a real bargain. Is it too early to say he's a candidate for signing of the season?

He's the biggest change to Brentford's starting XI but I'd wager late addition El Hadji Malick Diouf is likely to become a regular starter at left-back. Forward Jaidon Anthony has already started twice, Callum Wilson is proving why he's the perfect back-up (if not competitor) to Igor Thiago and centre-back Jannik Schuster provides cover, especially with Sepp van den Berg injured.

Plus, Brentford have managed to hold onto their key men. Jordan Henderson's leadership will be missed, but they've retained star attacking players Thiago, Kevin Schade and Yehor Yarmoliuk - someone who's really impressed bigger clubs recently - and tied down Michael Kayode and Vitaly Janelt with new contracts.

The only Deadline Day movement was the news that Jayden Meghoma went to Portsmouth on loan - a move in line with the club's determination to make sure their young players get game time.

I'm only avoiding giving Brentford a 10 because, as I'm sure Keith Andrews himself would say, there's always room for improvement!

It's been an uncharacteristically busy summer window for Brighton. The club have brought in nine players ready for the first team at a cost of nearly £170m. There is strength in depth in many areas - most notably in defence.

Luka Vuskovic came in for a club record £50m - something of a coup for the Seagulls. The arrival of young defensive midfielder Chema Andres from Stuttgart - a Spain U21 international - in a dramatic late twist on Deadline Day goes some way to filling the hole left by Carlos Baleba, who joined Manchester United.

He will need time to adapt to the Premier League but looks a real talent. They have lost a lot of experience and goal power in the shape of Danny Welbeck up front - they will be hoping loan signing Promise David can deliver on that front.

Liverpool target Yankuba Minteh is staying at the club. That should be considered significant for Brighton.

Once some of the injured players return and gel with the new signings, head coach Fabian Hurzeler will be hoping he has enough to successfully tackle the Premier League and Conference League.

Chelsea's squad has been revolutionised in this transfer window following a clear shift in strategy. Premier League-ready players have been brought in to complement the young, talented footballers already at the club. The pursuits of Jordan Henderson , Emiliano Martinez and Danny Welbeck marked a massive change from what we have seen from the club since the takeover.

Chelsea will continue to sign some of the best young players in world football, as seen with the arrival of Geovany Quenda . However, they have appreciated the need to bring in players who are ready to make an immediate impact.

They have also acted quickly to tie down Joao Pedro to an improved contract to ward off potential suitors. The core of this squad is here to stay.

Last season marked one of the worst in Chelsea's modern history. The campaign completely unravelled following Enzo Maresca's departure. The feeling was unsavoury amongst the fanbase despite a run to the FA Cup final.

The appointment of Xabi Alonso and a redefined recruitment policy has galvanised the supporters. Stamford Bridge felt alive again during their thrilling 4-3 victory over Brighton. There is plenty of work for Alonso to do on the pitch but things are looking bright.

The only sour note of the window has been the Enzo Fernandez saga. It has been a contentious issue which has left fans divided. Creating a deadline - set for 5pm on August 15 - didn't have the desired impact.

No guarantees were offered that the Argentina midfielder would remain and the uncertainty crept into the new campaign. However, a record of three wins from three matches would suggest that internally the squad have been unaffected.

In Emiliano Martinez, Morgan Rogers and Maxence Lacroix , Chelsea have signed three players who immediately strengthen their starting XI.

Losing Marc Cucurella was a blow but one of a number of impressive sales. The club succeeded in achieving their high valuation for players surplus to requirements, such as Liam Delap , Nicolas Jackson and Alejandro Garnacho .

Chelsea have proven to be world-class player traders in recent years. The question now will be whether they can deliver world-class results on the pitch.

Coventry had an ambitious summer. They spent big but there has been a clear plan behind it, mixing Premier League experience with younger signings who can grow with the club.

The biggest improvement is the depth available to Frank Lampard. Carl Rushworth has returned permanently after playing such a big role in last season's promotion, while Aurele Amenda adds athleticism at centre-back. Caleb Yirenkyi is an exciting signing in midfield, with Frank Onyeka bringing Premier League experience and Gustavo Hamer adding familiarity and creativity.

Up front, Taiwo Awoniyi gives Coventry a proven Premier League focal point, while Loum Tchaouna and Sidiki Cherif add pace and potential.

Questions remain about whether the new-look attack will produce enough goals, particularly after two defeats without scoring to start the season, but the squad is unquestionably stronger and has far more depth than the one that won promotion.

For a newly promoted side, Coventry have been bold without looking reckless. A very strong window with a serious statement of intent.

In Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Munoz , it is without doubt that Crystal Palace lost two of their best players this summer.

But Palace will see keeping hold of Adam Wharton , Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr as a big win.

Mateta got over transfer heartbreak last January when a move to AC Milan fell through and he may need to coach his team-mate Sarr through the next few months after Liverpool's efforts to sign him didn't come off.

Mateta himself is in the last year of his contract, but are we just four months away from another window where his future is up for speculation?

Sarr's performances from now until January will determine whether Palace's strong stance on him staying was correct.

Palace, as is the norm, have had to try to be clever in the market. Their signings have been sensible rather than sensational.

Axel Disasi , Dwight McNeil , Ben Chilwell and Takehiro Tomiyasu are all very capable Premier League players.

Dario Osorio could be the gem. The 22-year-old comes highly rated and Palace have a habit of unearthing big talents. Honest Ahanor is young but is a good addition at the back.

Time will tell, but Anan Khalaili looks like he has the potential to eventually fill Daniel Munoz's shoes.

Overall, Palace finished the window with better depth than they started, which is crucial for another season with European football.

They've become experts at losing big players and dealing with it. Michael Olise, Eberechi Eze and Marc Guehi have left and Palace have not just survived but thrived.

Palace will be an interesting story. You can't say their business this summer guarantees success. But a late flurry of deals, matched with early considered signings, makes one feel they'll be satisfied with the window.

That's Everton that! But how have they got to a situation where they've halved a strike force that was far from prolific anyway?

Easy to say in hindsight but allowing Beto to go to Fiorentina before a deal for Folarin Balogun was signed and sealed now looks amateur at best. The unsuccessful pivot to Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee when the Balogun deal initially faltered just adds to the feeling of a chaotic and panicked end to the window.

Add to that the sale of their most exciting talent, Iliman Ndiaye . All window, it was emphasised Everton were in a position of strength given he had three years left on his contract. Yet a deal to sell was struck at £65m . Over four times the amount Everton paid two years ago but not the figure that would have made it that bit more palatable for the fans.

Of course Ndiaye was initially off to Spurs for £60m with Richarlison coming the other way for £35m. A fee for the Brazilian that, even taking into account the esteem in which he's held by the blue half of Merseyside, appeared to be on the high side and ultimately was the first of Everton's proposed Deadline Day deals to fall through.

Kenny Tete was another. Fulham weren't letting him go without knowing they definitely had a replacement - a lesson in that, perhaps. So a tumultuous end to a window that has been far from easy when you consider the club's ownership mulling over Nottingham Forest's £40m offer to buy Harrison Armstrong at a time when David Moyes was talking up the need for getting players in.

And Evertonians could do with some positivity. At the moment, they are hurt, embarrassed, angry, frustrated and concerned, when the facts are that it didn't need to be like this.

Ainsley Maitland-Niles, Jack Grealish , Hayden Hackney , Christian Norgaard , Merlin Rohl , Tyrique George and Brennan Johnson have all arrived.

Unfortunately, the positives are more than overshadowed by the fact that the manager has, again, not been given the tools that will give him the best chance of delivering success.

Last season it was the failure to bring in a right-back and a proven striker. This season he has to muddle through until at least January with Thierno Barry as his only recognised front man.

Given the circumstances, it's difficult to see them muster a challenge for Europe - and if that is the case it shouldn't be seen as a failure.

For Fulham, the real proof will be in the eating over the next few months. With Alvaro Arbeloa looking to introduce a new high-pressing, high-tempo approach at Craven Cottage, there will inevitably be a bedding-in period.

But on paper, Fulham have addressed several of the key areas they needed to strengthen.

The biggest requirement was a quality striker and in Gonzalo García , arriving from Real Madrid, they appear to have found one.

His early return is certainly encouraging, scoring twice in his first three games.

The midfield has also been significantly strengthened. Fulham have added two more Real Madrid academy graduates in Cesar Palacios and Manuel Angel , while Shea Charles arrives from Southampton and Hugo Larsson from Eintracht Frankfurt.

That gives Arbeloa considerably more depth and variety in the middle of the pitch, with a mixture of energy, technical quality and flexibility. The biggest question mark remains at the back.

We have already seen Fulham exposed defensively and that is perhaps an inevitable consequence of Arbeloa's philosophy. His centre-backs are being asked to defend higher up the pitch, while the full-backs are encouraged to push even further forward.

That makes the Deadline Day signing of David Affengruber particularly interesting. The Austria international's profile appears well suited to Arbeloa's demands and his ability to defend space could prove valuable in a system that asks so much of its defenders.

Despite losing Harry Wilson and Samuel Chukwueze , Fulham have not signed a winger in this window. That is a surprise and will leave some fans concerned. Palacios - who started on the left wing against Chelsea and Sunderland - is not a specialist winger.

Nonetheless, Fulham's summer business feels ambitious. They have recruited players who fit the manager's vision, rather than just filling gaps in the squad.

If Arbeloa can get the balance right between aggression and defensive security, Fulham have the ingredients to avoid a relegation battle.

Hull were looking to add pace, athleticism and quality to their squad in this window - and they've certainly achieved that.

Eighteen new players have arrived, including six on Deadline Day. Owner Acun Ilicali has played a key role in the recruitment process, convincing prospective signings of the club's huge ambition. And there is a feeling that a patient approach has helped them to land their primary targets on favourable terms.

The club has added strength in depth, with young players targeted who can develop and improve with the club. Although that approach does bring an element of risk, it also offers huge reward if they are successful.

The starting XI has been improved but significantly, the core of the side that helped Hull achieve promotion remains, with an emphasis on retaining that spirit which could be so important to the club's survival hopes in a tough Premier League season.

Ipswich can look back on an extremely busy summer transfer window, with 14 incomings and 18 departures, as one that certainly suggests they have learnt from two years ago.

Approximately £110m was spent in the summer of 2024 to try and help the club remain a Premier League side. That failed, but fast-forward two years and £200m spent in this window, topped up by the Deadline Day signing of Zian Flemming from Burnley, and the club are certainly showing their ambition.

They've added experience, physicality and Premier League know-how, while bringing in players with the potential to grow into major assets for the club.

Julio Enciso has arrived as a record signing, while Abdul Fatawu , Emersonn and Exequiel Palacios add real quality and attacking threat. Sasa Lukic , Issa Diop and Florentino Luis also bring Premier League experience , while Daizen Maeda brings pace and proven pedigree.

What stands out is the depth Ipswich now have across the squad. They haven't simply replaced players - they have strengthened almost every area. It's now down to Gary O'Neil to gel the group together quickly and continue what's been an encouraging start to the new campaign.

All the focus will understandably be on the success story of Leeds' Deadline Day - and how different it feels to 12 months ago when they missed out on Harry Wilson at the last minute - but the most crucial part of their business was done earlier in the summer.

By signing Wilson, Tarik Muharemovic and James Trafford , Daniel Farke has upgraded three key positions. The Leeds manager has been keen to improve the individual quality in his squad and this trio does that. All of them make his starting XI better.

Signing those three would not have been enough though. Leeds had a squad depth issue last season and by signing Nico Elvedi , Michael Zetterer and Melvin Bard, they have begun to properly address that.

The last man through the door, Jean-Matteo Bahoya , is the wild card. The winger provides an X factor and lightning-quick pace that make him a potential game-changing signing. It is up to him now to see if he can deliver on that promise.

If we revisit 12 months down the line and Bahoya is a hit, Leeds' window goes up another level. Regardless, the hierarchy at Leeds have delivered a squad capable of achieving their goal of consolidating their place in the Premier League.

Liverpool have ticked a number of boxes that many will have seen as a priority.

Pace in the wide attacking areas has been addressed with the signings of Bradley Barcola and Victor Munoz .

In turn, with Cody Gakpo staying (he was never going to be sold after Liverpool were knocked back in approaches for Yankuba Minteh and Ismaila Sarr ), Andoni Iraola now has four wide options to choose from when you add the emerging talent of Rio Ngumoha to that. He also retains Gakpo as a possible backup to Alexander Isak with Hugo Ekitike still injured.

They've strengthened at the back with Ronald Araujo able to cover both centre-back and right-back. A crucial addition given the injuries to Joe Gomez , Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni . Araujo also approaches the game in a way that contrasts yet complements that of Jeremy Jacquet , whose deal was sorted in the winter window before signing this summer, and who already looks the part as a Liverpool centre-half.

On the flip side, when one of the priorities was to fill the position vacated by Mohamed Salah , Liverpool have not been able to bring in a naturally right-sided winger even though Barcola, Gakpo, Ngumoha and Munoz have all played out there at various points in their career.

I agree with those who feel that at least another quality full-back option and a holding midfielder would have made a massive difference to this squad's potential.

Barcola brings undoubted star quality. Munoz looks like he has the mentality to thrive, while Jacquet's style, coupled with Araujo's attitude, already resonates with the fans. So to deem this window a failure would be wrong.

The average age of Liverpool's first-team signings over the last two summer windows is around 22, which is another positive.

And in another nod to the future, they've been able to secure deals for two 18-year-olds in Lucca Brughmans and Djylian N'Guessan, who will join up properly in time for the start of next season.

At the same time, when the squad is not as well-rounded as it could be, there is an argument to say it could have been better.

It sounds a bit ridiculous to score Man City highly, given they had to allow Rodri , the best player at the World Cup, to leave for Barcelona. However, just as the fans were beginning to get restless, City managed to pull a couple of big-money irons from the dying embers of the transfer window.

Enzo Fernandez made all the headlines on a dramatic Deadline Day that saw them smash their transfer record for the second time this summer. He'll potentially partner Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi in a new-look £300m midfield that will be the envy of many around Europe.

Those close to the club are adamant the squad is in better shape now than it was at the start of last season, with the money received for Savio , Omar Marmoush , Nico Gonzalez , Tijjani Reijnders , Nathan Ake and James Trafford allowing them to also add Iliman Ndiaye and Allan to their attacking options.

Enzo Maresca has the tools he wanted for his revolution - time to see if it'll be enough to fight for the title.

Some may be surprised by me giving Manchester United a relatively high score in the transfer market - but let me explain my thought process.

United went into the window needing to rebuild their midfield. That was their priority, and three signings later, with around £155m spent, they have done that.

Andrey Santos , Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba will balance United's midfield alongside Kobbie Mainoo, and the combinations Michael Carrick now has at his disposal for the competitions they will compete in this season give room for optimism.

Yes, they did not get a left-back and it is clear they lack depth in that position - however, it is easy to forget they have players who can play in that position. Noussair Mazraoui deputised there well for Morocco in this summer's World Cup, while Diogo Dalot can also feature there.

Ultimately, United did not see the departures they perhaps imagined at the beginning of the window. Joshua Zirkzee , Manuel Ugarte and Marcus Rashford staying limited their ability to strengthen other positions.

However, if Rashford continues to build on his promising performances at the start of the season, he could be like a new signing for Carrick.

The summer transformation is complete at Newcastle, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo on Deadline Day becoming their eighth signing.

Of the eight, Lukas Hornicek , Amar Dedic , Nico Gonzalez and Fernandez-Pardo come into the strongest XI, but there's still so much headroom to improve for the likes of Sean Steur , Aladji Bamba , Bazoumana Toure and Ewan Jaouen , who are all very young and raw.

Newcastle have spent £262m this summer, having raked in £245m for Sandro Tonali , Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon .

They've beefed up the squad and made it youthful. But the last two signings of Gonzalez and Fernandez-Pardo for a combined £101m feel the most important. And the most ambitious.

For a window that at one stage looked as though it would be a disaster after a couple of early hijacks, Newcastle have turned the ship around.

And the early displays of Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa (who arrived for a combined £110m last summer) make the team feel like they have two more new signings.

A solid first window for new boss Oliver Glasner .

He wanted a physical No 9 with a high upside - he got that in Liam Delap . He wanted a starting-calibre wing-back - he got that by reuniting with Daniel Munoz . Ousmane Diomande was a Glasner target and the manager's also working again with Xaver Schlager after their time together at Wolfsburg.

The one slight on their summer business is failing to replace Elliot Anderson with a young, dynamic, forward-thinking midfielder. They did, however, get good money from Man City.

Sunderland left it until the dying moments of Deadline Day to add the winger that they had wanted all window.

They didn't originally want Malick Fofana , but they worked their way down the list until Fofana was the best option with less than 24 hours to go.

But the Lyon winger made it difficult for them, and a crazy tug-of-war between themselves and Crystal Palace ensued at Lyon airport.

It took Sunderland owner Kyril Louis-Dreyfus stepping in, throwing more money at the situation, and getting the deal over the line.

Fofana gets in Sunderland's starting XI - he has to for all that hassle getting the deal done.

So too does big summer signing Dayann Methalie . But the key for Sunderland this window has been holding onto their big-hitters like Granit Xhaka , Brian Brobbey and Noah Sadiki .

In terms of commitment to spending, it's 10/10. Tottenham kept their promise to spend big. But for the individuals, the jury is out at the moment, and Spurs are one of many clubs that have perhaps overpaid. So as it stands, a seven.

It's been a window unlike any I can remember. Spurs came out of the blocks with eye-opening signings, such as beating Manchester United to Mateus Fernandes and signing a player in Sandro Tonali that many would have thought out of their reach.

Roberto De Zerbi has been given the keys to reshape the Tottenham squad. A prime example is spending around £50m on Jan Paul van Hecke , who had only one year on his contract. That is something you would never expect from Spurs.

While the defence and midfield have been worked on, the clear issue last season was a lack of quality in the forward areas. The year-long pursuit of Savio finally came to a conclusion and he was joined by Omar Marmoush to the delight of the fans.

De Zerbi then told Sky Sports News he wanted one more big signing. That was believed to be Cody Gakpo - but City joined the race and it was clear that, if he were to leave, he would be going to Manchester.

After a disappointing defeat to Newcastle, Spurs fans woke up to another 'bomba', with a fee agreed with Everton for Iliman Ndiaye , and Richarlison going the other way. This is a player who would have got bums off seats. But on Monday, Ndiaye chose City and Richarlison publicly criticised the club.

Spurs then contacted rivals Chelsea for Mykhailo Mudryk and Tosin Adarabioyo . Mudryk's arrival signifies the board and scouting department have given De Zerbi full backing.

Spurs and Chelsea do not do business. Times are changing, finances are changing, board members change. Mudryk is a big risk - he hasn't played competitive football in nearly two years.

But if De Zerbi can get the best out of him, it could prove to be a shrewd signing. Chelsea's insistence of a high loan-to-buy fee shows they haven't totally given up on Mudryk either.
